newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-KUERTEN RISES TO BIG OCCASION.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KUERTEN RISES TO BIG OCCASION.

text.p: Gustavo Kuerten became the first Brazilian man to reach a Grand Slam final when he romped to a four-set win over Filip Dewulf at the French Open on Friday.
In front of a sparse Roland Garros crowd, the wiry Brazilian, ranked 66 in the world, overcame Dewulf, a Belgian qualifier world ranked 122, 6-1 3-6 6-1 7-6.
The 20-year-old will meet either Sergi Bruguera of Spain or Australian Pat Rafter in Sunday's final.

"I can't believe it's real, maybe God is from Brazil," said Kuerten, kitted out from head to foot in yellow and blue much to the chagrin of French Open officials who have pleaded with him to wear more traditional whites.

Kuerten has survived three five-set matches on his way to the final and has upstaged proven clay-court experts such as Austrian Thomas Muster and Ukraine's Andrei Medvedev and defending champion Yevgeny Kafelnikov of Russia along the way.

Dewulf, the first qualifier in 20 years to reach the semifinals of a Grand Slam tournament, may not have provided Kuerten with his biggest test of the fortnight but it was certainly among the tensest.
Leading 5-4 in the fourth set and sitting on the brink of a place in the final, Kuerten failed to serve out for the match, Dewulf breaking him and eventually forcing a tie-break.

The match appeared to be heading to a fifth set until Dewulf put successive forehands into the net to hand Kuerten a 5-4 lead. The next point Kuerten watched the ball fall favourably off the net-cord and then Dewulf hit a long forehand to give the Brazilian the tie-break 7-4.
"Sometimes the ball touches the net, sometimes it happens against me, but this week it has always been in my favour," said Kuerten. "I was a little bit nervous on match point."

Win or lose, the Brazilian, who lists soccer and surfing as his favourite past-times away from the court, will be in for the biggest pay day of his career, the $600,000 in first prize money more than doubling his $284,000 career earnings.
If Kuerten's appearance in the final is being greeted with relative indifference in Paris it is a different story back in Brazil where he is quickly becoming a national hero.

"My mother came from Brazil yesterday and she says it's unbelievable in my home town," said Kuerten, who lives in Florianopolis. "There's no one on the streets when I play and when I win everyone goes out on the streets to celebrate."
